stem: EMI — Study designs: A researcher wants to investigate the relationship between childhood adversity and adult depression. She recruits 200 adults with major depressive disorder and 200 age- and sex-matched controls from primary care, then retrospectively enquires about adverse childhood experiences using a validated questionnaire. Which study design is this?
distractors_rationale: Cross-sectional studies assess exposure and outcome simultaneously at a single time point, not retrospectively from outcome to exposure.
A prospective cohort study would follow participants forward in time from exposure to outcome, not recruit based on outcome status.
Retrospective cohort studies identify a historical cohort based on past exposure and follow up to outcome — this study recruits based on outcome (depression vs no depression), not exposure.
RCTs involve random allocation to an intervention, not retrospective exposure ascertainment.
Ecological studies use group-level rather than individual-level data.
Qualitative studies explore subjective experiences using interviews or focus groups, not quantitative exposure-outcome associations.
Case series describe a group of patients with the same condition without a comparison group.
Crossover trials involve each participant receiving both interventions in sequence, not relevant here.
A nested case-control study draws cases and controls from within an existing cohort, but the described design is a standard case-control study.
teaching_point: In a case-control study, participants are selected based on outcome status (cases with the disease vs controls without), and exposure is retrospectively ascertained. This design is efficient for rare outcomes and when the latency between exposure and outcome is long. The key limitation is recall bias — cases may differentially recall exposures compared with controls. Reference: BMJ 2008;337:a1022.
source: SPMM EMI Research Methods; BMJ Evidence-Based Medicine

stem: EMI — Study designs: A research team wants to determine whether a new online CBT programme reduces depressive symptoms compared with treatment as usual. They randomly allocate 300 patients with mild-to-moderate depression to receive either the online CBT programme or continue with their GP's usual care, then measure PHQ-9 scores at 12 weeks. Which study design is this?
distractors_rationale: Case-control studies select based on outcome; this study randomises to intervention groups.
Cross-sectional studies measure at one time point; this study follows up over 12 weeks.
Prospective cohort studies do not involve random allocation — participants are followed forward without random assignment.
Quasi-experimental designs lack random allocation; this study explicitly randomises.
Crossover trials give each participant both interventions sequentially; this is a parallel-group design.
Factorial designs test two or more interventions simultaneously in a single trial with multiple arms.
Cluster randomised trials randomise groups (e.g., GP practices) rather than individuals.
N-of-1 trials involve single participants receiving alternating treatments.
Pragmatic trials are a subtype of RCT designed to test real-world effectiveness rather than explanatory efficacy — the core design is still an RCT.
teaching_point: This is a parallel-group RCT — the gold standard for establishing treatment efficacy. Random allocation minimises confounding by distributing known and unknown prognostic factors evenly between groups. Key quality markers include allocation concealment, blinding (where possible), and intention-to-treat analysis. Reference: CONSORT 2010 statement, BMJ 2010;340:c332.
source: SPMM EMI Research Methods; CONSORT guidelines

stem: EMI — Study designs: A psychiatrist sends a questionnaire to all consultant psychiatrists in her trust asking about their current prescribing practices for antipsychotic polypharmacy. All responses are collected within a single 4-week period. Which study design is this?
distractors_rationale: Case-control studies compare cases with controls based on outcome status.
Prospective cohort studies follow participants forward over time.
Retrospective cohort studies look back at historical data from existing records.
Ecological studies use groups rather than individuals as the unit of analysis.
Survey is a data collection method, not a study design per se — the design is cross-sectional if data are collected at one point in time.
Qualitative studies explore meanings and experiences using non-numerical data.
Longitudinal studies involve repeated measurements over time, which is not the case here.
Case series describe clinical features of a group of patients with the same condition.
Comparative study is a broad term; the specific design here is cross-sectional.
teaching_point: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome simultaneously at a single time point. It is useful for determining prevalence but cannot establish temporality (which came first, exposure or outcome). Surveys are commonly cross-sectional in design. Reference: BMJ 2012;344:e3677.

stem: EMI — Study designs: A researcher follows a group of 500 first-episode psychosis patients for 5 years after their initial presentation, recording medication adherence, relapse rates, and functional outcomes as they naturally occur in routine clinical care. No intervention is introduced by the researcher. Which study design is this?
distractors_rationale: Retrospective cohort studies use existing records rather than following participants forward from baseline.
Case-control studies select based on outcome, not exposure.
Cross-sectional studies measure at one time point, not over 5 years of follow-up.
Naturalistic observational study describes the approach but 'prospective cohort study' is the formal design name.
Longitudinal case series lack a defined comparison group and typically describe outcomes without analytical comparisons.
RCTs require random allocation to an intervention.
Quasi-experimental studies involve a non-randomly allocated intervention or exposure.
Nested case-control studies draw cases from within an existing cohort — the parent design is still a cohort.
Qualitative studies use interviews and thematic analysis.
teaching_point: This is a prospective cohort study: participants are identified at baseline and followed forward in time to observe outcomes. The key strength is the ability to establish temporality and calculate incidence rates. The key limitation is attrition (loss to follow-up). Cohort studies are ideal for studying prognosis and natural history of disease. Reference: BMJ 2009;339:b2535.

stem: EMI — Study designs: A qualitative researcher interviews 15 people with lived experience of borderline personality disorder about their experiences of accessing mental health services. She uses thematic analysis to identify common themes in their accounts. Which type of study is this?
distractors_rationale: Phenomenological studies focus specifically on the lived experience of a phenomenon, not the broader service access experience.
Grounded theory aims to develop theoretical explanations from data, not simply identify themes.
Cross-sectional studies measure numeric variables; this is qualitative.
Case series describe clinical features of patients; this explores subjective experiences.
Surveys collect structured numerical or categorical responses from larger samples.
Mixed methods combines qualitative and quantitative approaches; only qualitative is described here.
Case-control studies compare exposures between groups with and without an outcome.
Narrative analysis focuses specifically on story structure and sequencing.
Discourse analysis examines language use and social construction of meaning.
teaching_point: Thematic analysis is a widely used qualitative method that involves identifying, analysing, and reporting patterns (themes) within data. It differs from grounded theory (which aims to generate theory) and phenomenological approaches (which focus on the essence of lived experience). Qualitative studies are suited to exploring experiences, beliefs, and processes that cannot be quantified. Reference: Braun V, Clarke V. Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qual Res Psychol 2006;3(2):77-101.
source: SPMM EMI Research Methods; Braun & Clarke 2006

stem: EMI — Sampling methods: An addictions researcher wants to study the injection practices of heroin users who are not in contact with treatment services. She recruits one participant from a needle exchange programme who then introduces her to three other users, who each introduce her to more participants. Which sampling method is this?
distractors_rationale: Convenience sampling selects easily available participants but does not involve participant referrals.
Purposive sampling selects participants deliberately for specific characteristics, not through chain referral.
Systematic sampling uses every nth person from a sampling frame.
Stratified random sampling divides the population into strata and randomly samples from each.
Simple random sampling gives every individual an equal probability of selection.
Quota sampling fills predefined quotas from subgroups non-randomly.
Cluster sampling randomly selects groups (clusters) and includes all members.
Consecutive sampling includes every consecutive eligible individual presenting to a service.
Volunteer sampling relies on self-selection, not chain referral.
teaching_point: Snowball sampling (also called chain-referral sampling) is used when the target population is hidden or hard to reach, such as illicit drug users, sex workers, or undocumented migrants. One participant recruits others from their social network. The limitation is that the sample may be biased towards more socially connected individuals. Reference: Heckathorn DD. Respondent-driven sampling. Sociol Methodol 1997;27(1):193-239.

stem: EMI — Sampling methods: A researcher wants to estimate the prevalence of PTSD among survivors of a major transport disaster. He selects every 10th name from the official survivor register compiled by the emergency services. Which sampling method is this?
distractors_rationale: Simple random sampling requires a random number generator or lottery method, not a fixed interval.
Stratified random sampling requires dividing into subgroups before random sampling.
Cluster sampling randomly selects groups, not individual names from a register.
Convenience sampling selects whoever is easiest to access, not from a systematic interval.
Purposive sampling deliberately selects specific individuals based on criteria.
Quota sampling fills non-randomly selected quotas from subgroups.
Snowball sampling uses chain referral from existing participants.
Consecutive sampling includes every individual in order of presentation.
Multistage sampling involves multiple levels of random selection (e.g., areas then individuals).
teaching_point: Systematic sampling selects every nth individual from a sampling frame. It is simple and efficient but can introduce bias if there is periodicity in the list (a pattern that coincides with the sampling interval). Systematic sampling is generally considered a non-random method as not every individual has an equal probability of being selected. Reference: BMJ 2014;348:g7610.

stem: EMI — Sampling methods: A research team wants to study the prevalence of depression across all GP practices in a region. Due to resource constraints, they randomly select 10 GP practices and then invite ALL registered patients in those practices to participate. Which sampling method is this?
distractors_rationale: Stratified random sampling would involve randomly sampling within each stratum, not including all members of selected groups.
Multistage sampling would involve random sampling at two or more levels (e.g., random practices then random patients within practices).
Simple random sampling selects individuals randomly from the entire population, not groups.
Systematic sampling uses fixed intervals from a list.
Convenience sampling selects whatever is easiest, not randomly selected clusters.
Purposive sampling selects specific individuals or groups deliberately.
Quota sampling fills predefined non-random quotas.
Consecutive sampling includes consecutive attendees, not all members of selected groups.
Snowball sampling uses participant referrals.
teaching_point: Cluster sampling uses naturally occurring groups (GP practices, schools, postcode areas) as the sampling unit. All members of randomly selected clusters are included. It is efficient when the population is geographically dispersed, but the design effect (inflation of variance due to clustering) must be accounted for in analysis. If individuals were also randomly selected within clusters, this would become multistage sampling. Reference: BMJ 2013;347:f6328.

stem: EMI — Bias in research: A researcher compares the effectiveness of a new antidepressant versus placebo. Patients who experience more side effects (and therefore correctly guess they are on the active drug) report better outcomes, partly because of their expectation of benefit. Which type of bias is this?
distractors_rationale: Detection bias refers to systematic differences in how outcomes are assessed between groups.
Selection bias refers to systematic differences between groups at baseline.
Attrition bias refers to systematic differences in who drops out of a study.
Recall bias refers to differential recall of past events between groups.
Publication bias refers to studies with positive results being more likely to be published.
Observer bias refers to researchers' expectations influencing outcome measurement.
Confounding by indication occurs when the reason for treatment is associated with the outcome.
Hawthorne effect refers to behaviour change due to awareness of being observed.
Lead-time bias refers to artificial inflation of survival time due to earlier diagnosis.
teaching_point: Performance bias arises when participants or personnel are aware of treatment allocation, leading to differential behaviours and expectations that can influence outcomes. This is why double-blinding is critical in RCTs — it minimises both performance and detection bias. When blinding is not possible (e.g., in psychotherapy trials), active control conditions or sham procedures should be used. Reference: Higgins JPT et al. Cochrane Handbook, Chapter 8: Assessing risk of bias.

stem: EMI — Bias in research: In a case-control study of the link between cannabis use and psychosis, patients with first-episode psychosis are more likely than healthy controls to search their memory for past cannabis use and report it in detail (perhaps exaggerating), while controls may under-report due to social desirability. Which type of bias is this?
distractors_rationale: Selection bias in case-control studies relates to how cases and controls are chosen, not how exposure is recalled.
Performance bias relates to differential behaviours due to knowledge of group allocation.
Detection bias relates to differences in how outcomes are measured or identified.
Attrition bias relates to systematic differences in who completes the study.
Publication bias relates to what gets published, not what gets recalled.
Interviewer bias relates to how researchers elicit information from participants.
Lead-time bias relates to earlier diagnosis falsely appearing to prolong survival.
Confounding by indication relates to treatment decisions being influenced by prognosis.
Berksonian bias is a selection bias in hospital-based case-control studies due to differential admission rates.
teaching_point: Recall bias is a systematic error in which participants do not remember past events accurately or differentially report them based on their outcome status. Cases (those with the disease) may think more about potential causes and therefore recall exposures more completely than controls. This is a key limitation of retrospective case-control studies. Reference: Althubaiti A. Information bias in health research. J Multidiscip Healthc 2016;9:211.

stem: EMI — Bias in research: A systematic review of antidepressant trials includes only published studies and finds a strong treatment effect. However, there are several unpublished trials showing no benefit of the antidepressant over placebo, which are not included in the analysis. Which type of bias does this represent?
distractors_rationale: Reporting bias refers to selective reporting of outcomes within a study, not non-publication of whole studies.
Selection bias relates to baseline differences between groups.
Attrition bias relates to differential dropout from studies.
Detection bias relates to differential outcome assessment.
Performance bias relates to knowledge of treatment allocation affecting behaviour.
Citation bias refers to selective citing of positive studies, a related but distinct concept.
Language bias refers to excluding studies published in languages other than English.
Confirmation bias refers to researchers seeking evidence that confirms their hypothesis.
Spin bias refers to presenting results in a way that overstates treatment benefits.
teaching_point: Publication bias (also called the 'file-drawer problem') occurs when studies with positive or statistically significant results are more likely to be published than those with null or negative results. This can seriously distort meta-analytic conclusions. Funnel plots and Egger's test are used to detect publication bias. The requirement for prospective trial registration (e.g., ClinicalTrials.gov) helps address this. Reference: Egger M et al. Bias in meta-analysis detected by a simple, graphical test. BMJ 1997;315:629.
source: SPMM EMI Research Methods; Egger et al. 1997

stem: EMI — Eating disorders: A 16-year-old girl with BMI 14.2 kg/m² presents with intense fear of weight gain, restrictive eating, and amenorrhoea for 6 months. She has lanugo hair on her arms and back, and peripheral oedema. Which diagnosis is most likely?
distractors_rationale: Binge-eating/purging type anorexia involves binge eating or purging behaviours, not purely restrictive eating.
Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent binge eating with compensatory behaviours, typically BMI ≥ 18.5.
Atypical anorexia nervosa includes all features of anorexia but weight is within or above normal range.
ARFID involves restricted eating without body image disturbance or fear of weight gain.
Binge eating disorder involves recurrent binge eating without compensatory behaviours.
Body dysmorphic disorder involves preoccupation with perceived flaws in appearance.
Orthorexia is a pathological obsession with healthy eating, not an official DSM-5 diagnosis.
Rumination disorder involves repeated regurgitation of food.
Purging disorder involves purging without binge eating, but the low BMI and amenorrhoea point to anorexia.
teaching_point: Anorexia nervosa restrictive type is characterised by low BMI (< 18.5, severe < 15), intense fear of weight gain, body image disturbance, and — in post-menarchal females — amenorrhoea. Physical signs include lanugo, bradycardia, hypotension, and peripheral oedema (refeeding risk). ICD-11 requires BMI < 18.5; severity is graded by BMI. Reference: NICE CG69 (2017 update); ICD-11 diagnostic criteria.

stem: EMI — Eating disorders: A 22-year-old university student with BMI 21.3 kg/m² presents with recurrent episodes of eating large amounts of food within a 2-hour period, accompanied by a sense of loss of control, occurring twice weekly for 3 months. She then induces vomiting and uses laxatives. She is extremely concerned about her shape and weight. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: OSFED — bulimia nervosa of low frequency/duration
distractors_rationale: Anorexia nervosa purging type requires low BMI (< 18.5); this patient has BMI 21.3.
Binge eating disorder involves binge eating without compensatory behaviours.
Purging disorder involves purging without binge eating.
Bulimia nervosa of low frequency would apply if criteria are nearly met but frequency or duration is insufficient.
Atypical anorexia requires body image disturbance with weight in normal range, but no purging mentioned as prominent.
Emotional overeating is a symptom, not a discrete diagnosis.
Rumination disorder involves regurgitation without nausea or disgust.
Night eating syndrome involves evening hyperphagia and nocturnal eating.
Pica involves persistent eating of non-nutritive substances.
teaching_point: Bulimia nervosa (ICD-11/DSM-5) requires: (1) recurrent binge eating episodes (large amount + sense of loss of control), (2) recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviours (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, excessive exercise), (3) at least once weekly for 3 months, and (4) self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape/weight. Unlike anorexia, BMI is typically normal or overweight. Medical complications include electrolyte disturbances, dental erosion, and parotid enlargement. Reference: NICE CG69; ICD-11; BNF 2023.

stem: EMI — Eating disorders: A 14-year-old boy with no body image disturbance refuses to eat solid foods due to sensory sensitivity to texture, a fear of choking, and a complete lack of interest in eating. His BMI is 15.8 kg/m² and he requires nasogastric feeding. He has no fear of weight gain or shape/weight concerns. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Feeding difficulty due to medical condition
distractors_rationale: Anorexia nervosa requires body image disturbance and fear of weight gain, which are absent here.
Bulimia nervosa involves binge eating and compensatory behaviours.
Pica involves eating non-nutritive substances.
Rumination disorder involves repeated regurgitation.
OSFED atypical anorexia requires body image concerns with normal weight.
Feeding difficulty due to medical condition would require an identifiable medical cause.
Selective eating (subthreshold) is a childhood pattern that doesn't typically cause severe malnutrition requiring NG feeding.
Functional dysphagia involves fear of swallowing but not the full ARFID picture.
Social anxiety disorder involves fear of scrutiny in social situations, not primary food refusal.
teaching_point: ARFID (DSM-5/ICD-11) is characterised by restricted food intake leading to significant weight loss, nutritional deficiency, or dependence on supplements/enteral feeding, WITHOUT body image disturbance or fear of weight gain. Three presentations: (1) lack of interest in eating, (2) sensory sensitivity to food textures/smells, (3) fear of aversive consequences (choking, vomiting). ARFID is more common in males and in children with neurodevelopmental disorders. Reference: DSM-5; ICD-11; Thomas JJ et al. Int J Eat Disord 2017.
source: DSM-5; Thomas JJ et al. Int J Eat Disord 2017

stem: EMI — Statistical tests: A researcher wants to compare the mean scores on the PANSS (positive and negative syndrome scale) between two independent groups of patients with schizophrenia — one group receiving clozapine, the other receiving olanzapine. Which statistical test is most appropriate?
distractors_rationale: Paired t-test is used for within-subject comparisons (same participants measured twice), not between independent groups.
Mann-Whitney U test is the non-parametric alternative when data are not normally distributed — the question does not indicate a normality violation.
Chi-square test compares proportions/categorical variables, not means of continuous variables.
Fisher's exact test is used for 2×2 contingency tables when expected cell counts are < 5.
Pearson's correlation measures the strength of association between two continuous variables, not group differences.
Spearman's rank correlation is the non-parametric version of Pearson's.
One-way ANOVA compares means across three or more groups, not two.
ANCOVA compares means while adjusting for covariates — useful but not the simplest test for this comparison.
McNemar's test compares paired proportions.
teaching_point: The unpaired (independent) Student's t-test is used to compare the means of a continuous variable between two independent groups. Assumptions: (1) data are continuous, (2) normally distributed in each group, (3) homogeneity of variances. If normality is violated, the Mann-Whitney U test should be used instead. If comparing three or more groups, one-way ANOVA is appropriate. Reference: Field A. Discovering Statistics Using IBM SPSS Statistics. 5th ed. 2018.

stem: EMI — Statistical tests: A researcher measures depression severity using the HAM-D (continuous scale) in the same group of 40 patients before and after an 8-week course of CBT. Which statistical test is most appropriate?
distractors_rationale: Unpaired t-test compares independent groups, not the same participants before and after.
Mann-Whitney U test is for independent groups, not paired comparisons.
Wilcoxon signed-rank test is the non-parametric alternative to the paired t-test when normality is violated.
Chi-square test compares categorical data, not continuous means.
McNemar's test compares paired categorical/proportional data.
Pearson's correlation measures association, not difference in means.
ANOVA compares means across 3+ groups.
ANCOVA adjusts for covariates.
Sign test is a non-parametric test for paired data but has less power than the paired t-test for continuous data.
teaching_point: The paired (dependent) t-test is used when the same participants are measured twice (before-after, or matched pairs). It accounts for the correlation between paired observations, making it more powerful than the independent t-test for detecting change. The non-parametric alternative is the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Assumptions: normally distributed differences. Reference: Altman DG. Practical Statistics for Medical Research. 1991.

stem: EMI — Statistical tests: A researcher wants to compare the prevalence of metabolic syndrome between 60 patients taking antipsychotics and 60 age-matched controls. Prevalence is a binary (yes/no) outcome. Which statistical test is most appropriate?
distractors_rationale: Student's t-test compares continuous means, not proportions.
Mann-Whitney U test compares distributions of ordinal or non-normal continuous data.
Paired t-test would be for a paired continuous comparison.
McNemar's test is for paired (dependent) proportions, not independent groups.
Fisher's exact test is used when expected cell counts are < 5 in a 2×2 table — not automatically the default for all 2×2 tables.
Logistic regression could also be used with adjustment for covariates, but for a simple two-group comparison of a binary outcome, chi-square is the standard first choice.
ANOVA compares means across groups.
Pearson's correlation measures linear association between two continuous variables.
Kappa measures inter-rater agreement, not group differences.
teaching_point: The chi-square test of association (χ²) is used to compare proportions between two or more independent groups. It tests whether there is a statistically significant association between two categorical variables. Assumptions: (1) independent observations, (2) no more than 20% of expected cell frequencies < 5 (otherwise use Fisher's exact test). For 2×2 tables, Yates' continuity correction is sometimes applied. Reference: Campbell MJ, Swinscow TDV. Statistics at Square One. 12th ed. BMJ Books.

stem: EMI — Statistical tests: A researcher recruits 50 patients with first-episode psychosis and measures their serum cortisol levels at baseline, then categorises them into 'remission' or 'non-remission' at 6 months. She wants to test whether baseline cortisol predicts later remission status, while adjusting for age and gender. Which statistical method is most appropriate?
distractors_rationale: Student's t-test compares means between two groups without adjusting for covariates.
Chi-square tests association between two categorical variables without covariate adjustment.
Pearson's correlation measures linear association between two continuous variables.
Linear regression requires a continuous outcome, not a binary one.
ANOVA compares means across groups without covariate adjustment.
ANCOVA adjusts for covariates but assumes a continuous outcome.
Factor analysis is a data reduction technique, not used for prediction with a binary outcome.
Survival analysis (Cox regression) is for time-to-event data, not a binary outcome at a fixed time point.
ROC curve analysis assesses diagnostic accuracy of a test — useful here but does not provide covariate adjustment.
teaching_point: Logistic regression is used when the outcome variable is binary (e.g., remission vs no remission). It can model the probability of the outcome given one or more predictor variables, and it allows adjustment for confounding variables (age, gender). Results are expressed as odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Multiple logistic regression enables simultaneous adjustment for several covariates. Reference: Hosmer DW, Lemeshow S. Applied Logistic Regression. 2nd ed. 2000.

stem: EMI — Child psychiatry: A 9-year-old boy with a long face, large ears, a prominent jaw, and enlarged testes is brought to CAMHS due to inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity at school. He also has anxiety and poor social skills. There is a family history of learning difficulties on the maternal side. Which diagnosis is most likely?
distractors_rationale: Down syndrome features include upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, flat nasal bridge, and a single palmar crease — not long face, large ears, or enlarged testes.
Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) presents in adolescence with tall stature, hypogonadism, and gynaecomastia — not with the classic facial dysmorphism described.
22q11.2 deletion syndrome involves cleft palate, cardiac abnormalities, and characteristic facial features (narrow palpebral fissures, bulbous nose) — not macrorchidism.
Angelman syndrome features include severe ID, ataxia, happy disposition, and microcephaly.
Prader-Willi syndrome features hypotonia, obesity, small hands/feet, and hyperphagia.
Williams syndrome features include elfin facies, cardiovascular abnormalities, and a friendly/inhibited social phenotype.
Tuberous sclerosis involves hamartomas, seizures, and ash-leaf macules.
Rett syndrome affects girls, with regression, hand-wringing, and microcephaly after normal early development.
Turner syndrome (XO) features short stature, webbed neck, and gonadal dysgenesis.
teaching_point: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, caused by CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene (X-linked). Physical features: long narrow face, large protruding ears, prominent jaw (macrognathia), and macro-orchidism (enlarged testes) post-puberty. Behavioural phenotype: ADHD, social anxiety, gaze aversion, and autistic features. It is associated with a high rate of ADHD and anxiety in childhood. Reference: Hagerman RJ et al. Fragile X syndrome. Nat Rev Dis Primers 2017;3:17015.

stem: EMI — Child psychiatry: A 6-year-old boy is brought to CAMHS with a history of normal development until age 14 months, then loss of previously acquired skills (speech, walking), and now exhibits hand-wringing stereotypies, bruxism (teeth grinding), and severe intellectual disability. He has a history of epilepsy with onset at age 3. His head circumference is below the 2nd percentile. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Cerebral palsy with associated intellectual disability
distractors_rationale: Rett syndrome occurs almost exclusively in girls, with regression between 6-18 months, loss of hand skills, and hand-wringing. This boy presents with a similar picture.
Childhood disintegrative disorder has regression after age 2 following a longer period of normal development.
Landau-Kleffner syndrome involves regression of language with epileptiform activity, not the full neurodevelopmental regression described.
Cerebral palsy is a static encephalopathy, not a regressive disorder.
Tuberous sclerosis involves hamartomas and characteristic skin lesions, not typically the regressive picture described.
MECP2 duplication syndrome affects boys with hypotonia, spasticity, and ID but typically without the period of normal early development.
West syndrome is an epileptic syndrome (infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia), not primarily a regressive genetic syndrome.
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is a severe childhood epilepsy syndrome.
CDKL5 deficiency causes early-onset epilepsy and severe ID but presents earlier (within weeks of birth).
teaching_point: Angelman syndrome is caused by deletion of the maternal 15q11-q13 region (UBE3A gene). Key features: (1) normal development until 6-12 months followed by regression, (2) severe intellectual disability, (3) ataxic gait, (4) frequent laughter/happy demeanour, (5) hand-flapping/hand-wringing stereotypies, (6) epilepsy (typically onset by age 3), (7) microcephaly by age 2. The 'Happy Puppet' phenotype is characteristic — frequent smiling, laughter, and excitability. Reference: Williams CA et al. Angelman syndrome. Nat Rev Dis Primers 2015;1:15028.
source: SPMM EMI Child Psychiatry; Williams et al. 2015

stem: EMI — Child psychiatry: An 8-year-old girl with a history of normal early development presents with episodic stereotyped hand-wringing movements, loss of purposeful hand skills between 6-18 months, severely impaired expressive and receptive language, and intellectual disability. She has microcephaly and a history of epilepsy starting at age 2. She is able to walk but has a wide-based gait. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Autism spectrum disorder with severe ID
distractors_rationale: Angelman syndrome is distinguished by frequent laughter and happy demeanour, not primarily the hand-wringing and regression seen here.
ASD with severe ID does not typically show the specific pattern of hand skill loss followed by stereotypic hand-wringing.
Childhood disintegrative disorder involves regression after at least 2 years of normal development.
Prader-Willi syndrome involves neonatal hypotonia, hyperphagia, and obesity, not this regressive picture.
CDKL5 deficiency causes early-onset epilepsy (within first weeks of life).
FOXG1 syndrome presents earlier with dyskinetic movements and postnatal microcephaly.
MECP2 duplication affects boys, not girls (MECP2 is X-linked — duplication in males is lethal, in females causes milder effects).
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is an epileptic syndrome, not a regressive disorder.
Dravet syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy) presents with prolonged febrile seizures in the first year of life.
teaching_point: Rett syndrome is an X-linked dominant neurodevelopmental disorder caused by MECP2 mutations, affecting almost exclusively girls (lethal in males). Diagnostic criteria (revised 2010): (1) regression followed by recovery/stabilisation, (2) partial/complete loss of purposeful hand skills, (3) gait abnormalities, (4) stereotypic hand movements. Supportive criteria: breathing irregularities, bruxism, scoliosis, epilepsy, microcephaly. After initial regression (typically 6-18 months), skills may partially plateau but do not progressively deteriorate. Reference: Neul JL et al. Rett syndrome: revised diagnostic criteria. Ann Neurol 2010;68(6):944-50.
source: SPMM EMI Child Psychiatry; Neul JL et al. 2010

stem: SBA — A 34-year-old woman with a history of multiple attendances to A&E presents with chronic feelings of emptiness, recurrent self-cutting to her forearms, and intense, unstable relationships. She describes a profound fear of abandonment and reports that her mood shifts rapidly from intense anger to despair within hours. She does not meet criteria for a current depressive or manic episode. Which of the following psychotherapies has the strongest evidence base for this condition?
distractors_rationale: CBT has evidence for BPD but has weaker evidence for reducing self-harm and suicidality compared with DBT.
MBT has evidence for BPD, particularly in specialist services, but DBT has the most robust evidence base for self-harm reduction.
TFP is a specialised psychodynamic approach for BPD but has less RCT evidence than DBT.
Schema therapy has emerging evidence for BPD but DBT remains the most established.
CAT has limited evidence specifically for BPD.
General psychodynamic psychotherapy has weak evidence for BPD compared with specialised approaches.
Behavioural activation is for depression, not BPD.
IPT is for depression, not BPD.
ACT is for anxiety and depression, not primarily for BPD with self-harm.
teaching_point: NICE CG78 (2009) recommends DBT for women with borderline personality disorder who present with recurrent self-harm. DBT combines individual therapy, group skills training, and phone coaching, targeting: (1) mindfulness, (2) distress tolerance, (3) emotion regulation, and (4) interpersonal effectiveness. The evidence from multiple RCTs shows DBT reduces self-harm, hospitalisations, and improves global functioning. MBT is an alternative evidence-based approach, but DBT has the most robust overall evidence. Reference: NICE CG78 (2009); Linehan MM et al. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2006;63(7):757-66.

stem: SBA — A 42-year-old man with no prior psychiatric history presents to the Emergency Department with acute severe anxiety, palpitations, sweating, trembling, a feeling of impending doom, and a sense that he is 'going crazy'. Symptoms began abruptly 40 minutes ago while shopping in a supermarket. He has no medical history, and ECG, bloods, and urine toxicology are normal. After 30 minutes, his symptoms resolve spontaneously without intervention. Over the following month, he presents twice more to the ED with identical episodes. He has become fearful of leaving his home and now avoids supermarkets entirely. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate diagnosis according to ICD-11?
distractors_rationale: Agoraphobia without panic disorder involves fear of situations without panic attacks themselves; this patient clearly has panic attacks.
GAD requires at least 6 months of persistent, generalised worry, not episodic attacks with full inter-episode recovery.
Panic disorder without agoraphobia would apply if there were no avoidance/escape-behaviour, but this patient now avoids supermarkets and going out.
Hyperventilation syndrome is not a primary psychiatric diagnosis in ICD-11.
Cardiac syndrome X is a cardiological diagnosis of exclusion, not a psychiatric condition.
Illness anxiety disorder involves preoccupation with having an illness despite negative medical workup.
Specific phobia — situational type involves fear of specific situations but without the episodic panic attack hallmark of panic disorder.
Acute stress reaction occurs within hours of an identifiable traumatic event and resolves within days.
teaching_point: ICD-11 panic disorder (episodic paroxysmal anxiety) requires recurrent unexpected panic attacks not restricted to specific situations, with persistent fear of recurrence or consequences. When this leads to avoidance of situations where escape might be difficult, agoraphobia is diagnosed concurrently. NICE CG113 recommends: (1) psychoeducation and monitoring (watchful waiting) for mild/subthreshold, (2) individual CBT-based self-help or brief CBT for mild/moderate, (3) more intensive CBT for moderate/severe, with SSRI (sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine) as second-line or when CBT is declined. Reference: NICE CG113 (2011); ICD-11.

stem: SBA — A 32-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of recurrent, intrusive thoughts that she has left the gas on in her house, causing her to return home repeatedly to check. The checking rituals take up to 2 hours per day, and she has been late for work on multiple occasions. She recognises the thoughts are excessive but cannot stop them. Attempts to resist the checking cause intense distress. She has no history of tics or body dysmorphic concerns. Which of the following treatment options should be offered FIRST according to NICE guidelines?
distractors_rationale: SSRI plus CBT is recommended as second-line or for moderate-to-severe cases, not first-line for mild-to-moderate OCD.
SSRI alone is less effective than combined treatment in moderate-to-severe OCD but is not the first step for mild-to-moderate cases.
Clomipramine is an alternative second-line if SSRI fails but has more side effects (anticholinergic, cardiotoxic).
Combined clomipramine and CBT is not first-line due to clomipramine's side-effect profile.
Deep brain stimulation is reserved for severe, treatment-refractory OCD.
TMS has emerging evidence but is not NICE-recommended first-line.
ACT and mindfulness have less evidence than ERP for OCD.
Psychodynamic psychotherapy has limited evidence for OCD.
teaching_point: NICE CG31 (2005) recommends a stepped-care approach: (1) mild impairment — individual or group CBT (ERP) with self-help materials; (2) moderate impairment — more intensive CBT (ERP), or offer SSRI if CBT is declined; (3) severe impairment — combined CBT (ERP) and SSRI. ERP involves graded exposure to feared situations (e.g., leaving gas unchecked) with response prevention (not performing the compulsion). The patient's degree of impairment (late for work, 2 hours/day) suggests moderate severity; CBT alone is still the first-line recommendation. Reference: NICE CG31 (2005); ICD-11.

stem: SBA — A 28-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by police after being found wandering the streets at night, confused and disoriented. He is unkempt, has a poor nutritional state, and appears profoundly apathetic. On examination, he has nystagmus on lateral gaze, ataxia, and cannot recall three objects after 2 minutes. He is unable to give any coherent history. His friend reports he is a heavy daily drinker and has recently stopped eating. Which of the following is the SINGLE most important immediate management step?
options: Administer oral thiamine 100 mg three times daily
Perform CT head scan before any treatment
Administer intravenous glucose 50 mL of 50% dextrose
Start IV fluids (normal saline) and monitor
Perform lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis
distractors_rationale: Oral thiamine 100 mg is for prophylaxis, not treatment of established Wernicke's encephalopathy — requires IV/Pabrinex.
CT head before treatment delays potentially life-saving intervention; treatment should not wait for imaging.
Chlordiazepoxide is for alcohol withdrawal but is not the immediate priority — Wernicke's treatment comes first.
Intravenous glucose without prior thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's encephalopathy by depleting thiamine stores.
MRI brain can confirm Wernicke's (T2 hyperintensities in mammillary bodies, thalamus, periaqueductal grey) but treatment must not be delayed for imaging.
IV fluids alone do not address the underlying thiamine deficiency.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated unless meningitis is suspected on fever/neck stiffness; there is no mention of infection.
IV haloperidol may worsen the situation; Wernicke's can cause confusion without psychosis requiring antipsychotics.
Naloxone is for opioid overdose, not relevant here.
teaching_point: Wernicke's encephalopathy is a medical emergency caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most commonly in alcohol-dependent patients with poor nutrition. The classic triad (confusion, ataxia, nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia) is present in only 16% of cases. NICE CG100 recommends: (1) immediate IV Pabrinex (one pair of high potency B-complex ampoules IV, three times daily for 3-5 days), (2) do NOT give glucose before thiamine, (3) treat on clinical suspicion alone — do not wait for investigations. Untreated, Korsakoff's syndrome develops in 80% of survivors. Reference: NICE CG100 (2010); Royal College of Physicians guidelines (2020).
source: NICE CG100; RCP guidelines; SPMM EMI Addiction

stem: SBA — A 68-year-old woman with a 2-year history of cognitive decline, including progressive memory loss and word-finding difficulties, is brought to clinic by her daughter. Over the past 6 months, she has developed visual hallucinations of 'small children playing in the garden', which she finds pleasant and non-threatening. She has had two unexplained falls in the last month. On examination, her BP is 130/85 lying and 115/70 standing; MMSE 21/30 — prominent deficits in attention and visuospatial function; she has subtle cogwheel rigidity in her right arm. Which of the following investigation findings would be MOST characteristic of the likely underlying pathology?
options: Reduced dopamine transporter uptake in the basal ganglia on DaTSCAN (FP-CIT SPECT)
Generalised cortical atrophy with medial temporal lobe predominance on MRI
Frontal and anterior temporal lobe atrophy on MRI
Multiple subcortical white matter hyperintensities on T2-weighted MRI
Reduced occipital glucose metabolism on FDG-PET
Elevated amyloid PET tracer uptake in frontal and parietal cortex
Reduced N-acetylaspartate on MR spectroscopy in the hippocampus
Prominent hippocampal atrophy on coronal MRI
distractors_rationale: Generalised cortical atrophy with medial temporal predominance is characteristic of Alzheimer's disease, not DLB.
Temporal lobe hypoperfusion on SPECT is more characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.
Frontal/anterior temporal atrophy suggests frontotemporal dementia.
Multiple white matter hyperintensities suggest vascular dementia (small vessel disease).
Reduced occipital glucose metabolism on FDG-PET is seen in DLB but is less specific than DaTSCAN.
Elevated amyloid PET tracer uptake confirms Alzheimer's pathology, not specific to DLB (DLB commonly has co-existent Alzheimer's pathology).
Reduced NAA on MRS is non-specific, seen in Alzheimer's.
Hippocampal atrophy is characteristic of Alzheimer's, not DLB.
Negative amyloid PET would argue against Alzheimer's but does not confirm DLB.
teaching_point: DLB is characterised clinically by the 4 core features: (1) fluctuating cognition with attentional deficits, (2) recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, (3) spontaneous parkinsonism, (4) REM sleep behaviour disorder. DaTSCAN (FP-CIT SPECT) shows reduced dopamine transporter uptake in the basal ganglia, which distinguishes DLB from Alzheimer's disease (> 80% sensitivity, > 90% specificity). Key management: avoid neuroleptic sensitivity (up to 50% develop severe, sometimes fatal, neuroleptic malignant-like reactions). Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine) improve cognition and behavioural symptoms. Reference: McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of DLB: Fourth consensus report. Neurology 2017;89(1):88-100.
